title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
The page closes §15, which derives the Euler–Lagrange equation for ∫Z dx with Z depending on x, y, p, q, r, s, …. The conclusion of §15 is that 0 = N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − d³R/dx³ + … is the sought relation between x and y. The 'absolute parts' are the integrated boundary terms from the previous page, of the form dt(dy/dt)(P − dQ/dx + …) + dt(d²y/dxdt)(Q − dR/dx + …) + …. Euler says these concern only the endpoints and are to be handled as explained elsewhere.

§16 sets aside the case where Z itself contains integral formulas (isoperimetric or nonlocal integrands), saying it has been treated elsewhere. Euler then announces a harder task: extending the new method, in which the variation is a differential with respect to an auxiliary parameter t, to functions of two variables. He admits he could not do this in his earlier dissertation on the calculus of variations, being 'deterred by the multitude of so many quantities of different kinds'. That earlier work is presumably the Elementa calculi variationum, E296.

§17 begins the two-variable application. A relation among x, y, z is read as a surface, with x and y horizontal and z vertical, so that z = z(x,y). The two partial increments are written dx(dz/dx) and dy(dz/dy), using Euler's parenthesis notation for partial derivatives. The next page introduces t, so that z = z(x,y,t) describes a one-parameter family of neighbouring surfaces, with δz represented by dt(dz/dt). This prepares the variational treatment of double integrals ∫∫V dx dy.

ideas.what: Euler–Lagrange equation for higher-order single-integral functionals; boundary terms affect only the endpoints
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Lagrange equation with natural/endpoint boundary terms
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi; E296 Elementa calculi variationum; E297

ideas.what: Integrands containing integral formulas (nonlocal Z) treated elsewhere
ideas.modern_name: Variational problems with integral-dependent integrands / isoperimetric-type functionals
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi (chapters on indeterminate integral formulae); E296/E297 (unsure of exact sections)

ideas.what: Programme of extending the parameter (t-)method of variation to functions of two variables, i.e. surfaces and double integrals
ideas.modern_name: Calculus of variations for multiple integrals; first variation via a one-parameter family z(x,y,t)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1760–61, Misc. Taurinensia, including the minimal surface equation); Euler's E420 is known as his own extension
ideas.where_published: E420 itself (Novi Comm. Petrop. 16, 1771/72); discussed in histories such as Goldstine's History of the Calculus of Variations and Fraser's papers

ideas.what: Partial-derivative notation (dz/dx) in parentheses for a surface z(x,y)
ideas.where_published: E212 Institutiones calculi differentialis and many papers

deep.surprise_reason: This is a transitional page: boundary terms deferred, nonlocal integrands deferred, and a programmatic announcement of the two-variable extension. Euler's candid admission that he earlier failed to handle the two-variable case is a nice historical remark, but E420's double-integral treatment is known and discussed in standard histories, and Lagrange had treated double integrals earlier. Nothing new here.
